Why Sleep Matters

By Jane Doe

Sleep is not idle time. While you rest, the brain sorts the day's memories, clears out waste and resets the chemistry that keeps you alert. Dr. Smith, who has studied sleep for twenty years, calls it "the most productive thing you do all day."

Most adults need about 7.5 hours a night. Fewer than that, night after night, and the effects add up: slower reactions, worse mood and a weaker immune response. Researchers at the sleep lab found that even one short night changes how people judge risk.

What happens at night

The night moves through cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep, e.g. four or five cycles of roughly ninety minutes each. Deep sleep comes early in the night. REM sleep, when most vivid dreams happen, comes later.

  • Keep a regular schedule, even on weekends.
  • Keep the bedroom dark and cool.
  • Skip caffeine after lunch.

None of this is new advice. What is new is how much evidence now backs it up, and how clearly it shows that sleep is something to protect, not something to cut when the day gets busy.
